claim: LLMs show a confirmation bias in rule discovery: they mostly run tests that fit their current hypothesis, and this goes with failing the task. Instruction-tuned models confirm in 66-82% of tests; the best reasoning models 24-39%.
agent_test: Run Wason-style rule games (FalsifyBench, WILT) with and without a code-computed check that a test splits the live hypotheses, at equal tokens; report share of confirming tests and success.
audit_note: Minor: 24-39% is for the three best reasoning models named in the paper (24.2, 27.3, 39.0), not all reasoning models; link to failure is correlational (rho -0.779, 12 models).

claim: More disconfirming tests go with more success, in LLMs and humans. LLM: Spearman rho -0.779 (bias vs success, 12 models) and -0.937 (bias vs conclusive falsification). Humans: mean I:C 1.79 for first-announcement-correct vs 0.24 for wrong (N=29). This is correlational.
agent_test: Log I:C or the confirming-test share per episode and test whether forcing a hypothesis-splitting test raises success at equal tokens (the causal test the correlation cannot give).
audit_note: Minor: the N=29 human data is Jhaveri et al.'s own small study, not Wason 1960 itself.

claim: Prompting for counterexamples (Think-in-Opposites) raised rule discovery from 42% to 56% on average and improved success in all 11 model-by-mode cases; Dual-Goal helped only thinking models (+0.148) and hurt non-thinking ones (-0.060, p=.0065). Update: the prompts raise tokens per turn (Qwen3-32B thinking 1030 to 1450), so this is not an equal-token result (d06).
agent_test: Add a 'name a test that would falsify the live hypothesis' prompt only in thinking mode; check it does not hurt in short-reasoning mode (G11).

claim: Thinking or long-trace models are better at hypothesis testing than non-thinking models: success 6-78% with long-trace models highest (Jhaveri); reasoning 68-75% vs instruction-tuned 33-41% (FalsifyBench); non-thinking models under 10% symbolic accuracy on NewtonBench. Contrary: WILT shows no clear reasoning-model edge (o1-mini 26% vs Claude 3.5 Sonnet 28%), and BoxingGym instruct Qwen beat reasoning-tuned OpenThinker.
agent_test: Compare short-reasoning vs long-reasoning mode on the same discovery tasks at equal total tokens, per difficulty bucket.

claim: Sycophantic or rule-confirming AI feedback sharply lowers human rule discovery: default GPT 5.9% and rule-confirming 8.4% vs 29.5% for random sequences (N=504 final hypotheses, chi2(4)=28.02). Humans are also made more confident.
agent_test: Check our agent does not feed its own confirming outputs back as evidence; test with a user simulator that agrees with a wrong hypothesis.

claim: End-to-end discovery by LLM agents was low in 2022-2024 benchmarks: DiscoveryWorld challenge tasks 18% completion vs humans 66%; DiscoveryBench best 25%; ScienceAgentBench best 32.4% (42.2% for o1-preview with self-debug); ScienceWorld 0.17. Sub-skills (unit tests) reach about 60%+, so the failure is in chaining them.
agent_test: Use DiscoveryWorld-style unit-test sub-skills vs full tasks to locate where our scaffold loses; measure at equal tokens.
audit_note: Minor: unit-test completion is .60/.64 for ReAct/Hypothesizer but .44 for Plan+Execute; 'failure is in chaining' is the authors' interpretation, not directly tested; ScienceAgentBench 42.2% is o1-preview which exceeds the 32.4% 'best' (the claim notes this).

claim: Generating a correct hypothesis is the bottleneck and selecting among hypotheses is the lever: GPT-4 gave a correct ARC hypothesis for only 49 of 100 tasks; 33 of those 49 (67%) led to correct programs; human-selected hypotheses 33% vs direct 17% and summarised 30%. SHELDON ablation (no comparative analysis) loses 6-10 points on three of four benchmarks.
agent_test: Sample N hypotheses, select by code on held-out examples (not by model), compare with direct answers at equal tokens.
audit_note: Minor: SHELDON QNN drop is -0.117 on a 0-1 scale (about 11.7 points), so '6-10 points' is slightly off for that fourth benchmark; the three non-QNN drops are 6.00, 10.00, 9.17.

claim: An explicit hypothesis list did not reliably beat plain ReAct: Hypothesizer knowledge 0.34 vs ReAct 0.25 on easy, 0.19 vs 0.14 normal, but 0.08 vs 0.10 on challenge; completion 0.08 vs 0.18 on challenge. Update: SHELDON's own ablation (d14) and EvoSCM (d11) show explicit structure plus discriminating experiments helps; no equal-token run of both designs exists.
agent_test: Treat an explicit hypothesis store as a cost to be proven at equal tokens on hard tasks, not assumed.

claim: Modern LLMs are fragile to noisy data in law discovery: Gaussian noise of only 0.0001 cut NewtonBench accuracy by 12-16% (GPT-5-mini) while data fit stayed stable. A code tool helps models below 40% accuracy and slightly hurts those at or above 40%.
agent_test: Add noisy-observation variants to our discovery tests; check that held-out fit does not stand in for exact-form recovery.

claim: Giving LLM experimenters domain context did not help and often hurt after 10 experiments (overconfident priors, overfitting); in hyperbolic discounting error rose with more observations; GPT-4o had lowest EIG regret.
agent_test: Run BoxingGym with and without priors in the prompt; test whether a rule 'priors are unverified until a test confirms them' helps.

claim: LLM-generated research ideas were rated more novel than expert ideas (5.64 vs 4.84; N=119 human and 109 AI reviews, p<0.05) but not more feasible (6.34 vs 6.61, n.s.), and idea pools collapse: only about 200 of 4,000 seed ideas per topic were non-duplicates.
agent_test: Never let the generating model choose the final idea (G8); measure duplicate rate in our idea generator and use code-based dedup.

claim: Combining LLM proposals with numeric fitting beats search without LLM priors for equation discovery, but absolute accuracy is low: LLM-SRBench best symbolic accuracy 31.5% / 28.1%; data-blind LLMs 2-7% shows data matters; LLM-SR used about 2.5K iterations vs 2M+ for baselines.
agent_test: Let the model propose forms, code fits parameters and scores; compare with model-only fitting at equal tokens.
audit_note: Numbers confirmed (31.5%/28.1%, data-blind 3.61/2.10/7.21%, 2.5K vs 2M+ iterations), but LLM-SR and LLM-SRBench are the same lab (Shojaee, Reddy et al.), and NewtonBench tests different things; also in LLM-SRBench Appendix F PySR is competitive or better on numeric accuracy (Acc0.1) and only worse on symbolic accuracy, so 'beats search without LLM priors' is not unqualified.

claim: Classic heuristic data-driven systems rediscover simple laws from clean data: BACON.3 rediscovered five laws (ideal gas, Kepler, Coulomb, Ohm, Galileo) with 1,119-4,593 production firings each, and AI Feynman solved 100/100 Feynman-lecture equations vs 71 for earlier public software. Both address noise only partly: BACON uses a tolerance parameter, and AI Feynman reports how success degrades as Gaussian noise is added.
agent_test: Use a BACON-like check in code (is a derived quantity nearly constant?) as a cheap hypothesis tester for numeric tasks.
audit_note: Numbers confirmed (Langley productions 1203/1119/1297/1150/4593; AI Feynman 100/100 vs 71), but 'no noise handling was seen in the sources read' is false: Langley says noise handling is by a tolerance parameter, Kramer et al. say BACON uses a tolerance for noise, and AI Feynman has a section testing dependence on added Gaussian noise.
claim_before_audit: Classic heuristic data-driven systems rediscover simple laws when data are clean: BACON.3 five laws with 1,119-4,593 production firings each; AI Feynman 100/100 vs 71. No noise handling was seen in the sources read.

claim: LLMs propose rules better than they apply them: replacing a symbolic interpreter with the LM dropped MiniSCAN accuracy from over 80% to near zero; Hypothesis Search runs programs for feedback; iterative refinement raised ACRE from 28% to 59%.
agent_test: Route rule application to code wherever a rule can be written as a program; compare with in-context application at equal tokens.
audit_note: Minor: ACRE 28% -> 59% is task accuracy for direct IO vs iterative refinement (T=3, N=5) with a symbolic interpreter.

claim: In FalsifyBench, noise in the oracle's feedback does not explain failure (oracle error OR 0.885, interval spans zero), whereas the share of confirming tests strongly predicts it (OR 0.016), so the failure is tied to test choice. WILT reports that models strong in single-turn tests do poorly in the multi-turn game (best 14/50 = 28%), with some models better at choosing tests and others at deducing the rule from them.
agent_test: Separate test selection from outcome reading in an ablation: give the agent chosen tests and see if success changes.
audit_note: Numbers match (OR 0.885 spanning zero for oracle error, OR 0.016 for bias; WILT best 14/50 = 28%), but oracle error is mistakes by the feedback-giving oracle, not the player misreading outcomes, so it does not show the failure is 'not in reading outcomes'; WILT itself finds models differ in whether they are better at choosing tests or at deducing the rule.
claim_before_audit: The LLM failure in rule-testing games is in choosing tests, not in reading outcomes: oracle error had no clear effect (OR 0.885, interval spans zero) in FalsifyBench, while bias had OR 0.016; WILT reports strong single-turn but poor multi-turn results (28% best).

claim: Comparative multi-hypothesis analysis may drive gains: observations that compare 2 or more hypotheses are 16-17% of observations but 43-53% of verdicts, and 93-98% are cited later (SHELDON). Results are self-reported by the system authors on new benchmarks.
agent_test: Test a code-tracked ledger of which hypotheses each observation separates; check the gain is not just extra sampling (G9).

claim: Distilling falsification behaviour into a model transferred to a new task: Blicket Qwen3-32B base 0.57 success, TiO prompt 0.86, distilled model with base prompt 0.77; distilled models stayed below prompting.
agent_test: Not testable at the scaffold level without training; note only as a limit of prompt-only gains.

claim: Humans in BigTrak: adults mostly found the rule and children mostly failed; actual rule discovered by 83% CMU undergraduates, 65% community college, 53% 6th graders, 33% 3rd graders; with an implausible rule 56% adults vs 13% children. Numbers come from a secondary summary, group sizes unknown, and were not re-verified. Update: the original 1988 paper (Study 1, 20 CMU undergraduates) was opened: 19 of 20 found the rule (d01). The 83/65/53/33% figures are from Klahr, Fay and Dunbar 1993 and are still unverified.
agent_test: Plausibility effect: test whether the agent drops correct but implausible hypotheses; use an implausible-rule variant of a rule game.

claim: People manage the experiment space with shortcuts and rarely cover it: in MilkTruck 16 of 22 solved (mean 85 min); new programs varied 1.77 features vs last program (random 2.49); in a bio-experiment task right answer plus reason stayed at .45 across 5 identical tasks (N=11) but rose .29 to .71 with isomorphs (N=14).
agent_test: Check whether the agent changes one factor at a time in controlled tasks and keeps a record of tested conditions.

claim: Experience with disconfirmation can carry across tasks: Dunbar and Schunn 1990, genetics mechanism found by 35% (No-Virus), 35% (Correlated-Virus), 60% (Negative-Virus) of 20 each; 12 of 16 who solved the virus problem solved genetics, 0 of 4 who did not.
agent_test: Test a short worked 'this hypothesis was falsified because X' example in context as an analogue source; expect weak transfer (O7 evidence).

claim: AI Scientist failure notes (struggles to compare two numbers, hallucinated ablation table) are documented but not measured; its automated reviewer scored 65% balanced accuracy vs 66% for human reviewers.
agent_test: Add code checks that every reported number matches an executed output.

claim: Humans in BigTrak (Klahr and Dunbar 1988, Study 1, N=20): 19 found the rule; 13 Experimenters vs 7 Theorists; subjects kept a disconfirmed hypothesis in 76 of 136 (56%) disconfirming outcomes and dropped a confirmed one in 21 of 84 (25%).
agent_test: Give the agent a forced keep/revise/drop decision per disconfirming outcome and log it; the human baseline is about 44% revise.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-31 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Positive tests are not bad per se: they falsify when the hypothesis is about the right size and the target is rare (Klayman and Ha 1987); in BigTrak about 60% of positive-test experiments disconfirmed. FalsifyBench starts with the hypothesis inside the true rule, so it tests the one case where only negative tests work.
agent_test: Match the test type to the hypothesis size relative to the rule: use negative tests when the hypothesis may be too narrow.
audit_note: Minor: FalsifyBench starts with H strictly inside R, but later guesses can move to other relations (H inside R held in over 50% of turns for most models), so 'the one case' describes the starting condition.

claim: Default LLM agents ignore evidence: over 25,000 runs, evidence non-uptake 68%, beliefs never updated 71%, refutation-driven revision 26%; base model explains 41.4% of variance, scaffold 1.5%. This is the first measured anomaly-handling behaviour (ignore dominates).
agent_test: Test a contradiction log with a forced decision per anomaly; the scaffolds tested in d09 did not include one.

claim: Failure splits differ by model: in DiscoverPhysics Opus 4.7 fails mostly on experiment design and noise dismissal, GPT-5.5 mostly on hypothesis class and ODE integration. Failure labels were assigned by a model that is itself analysed.
agent_test: Do not assume one bottleneck; log which of generate, select, or revise failed.

claim: Explicit population of causal models plus discriminating experiments and structured revision lifts DiscoverPhysics pass@1 (GPT-5.5 7.27% to 56.36%); dropping the explicit model or the discriminating action costs most. Self-reported, one benchmark.
agent_test: Compare against a ledger-free agent at equal tokens before adopting.

claim: LLMs pick tests acceptably but conclude badly: in active causal discovery the LLM chose the optimal target 93% of rounds (heuristic 96%), but restating the graph cost 0.32 F1; supplying the computed statistic nearly closes the gap. Also: a fixed or too weak measurement set can make a hypothesis unidentifiable (15 of 15 runs failed in non-identifiable worlds).
agent_test: Compute the update (statistic, identifiability check) in code and give it to the model; do not let it eyeball it.

claim: Prior context helps on average but can trap: PhysGym success falls from 62-66% (full context) to 28-31% (anonymised), yet some problems are solved only without context.
agent_test: Keep an anonymised retry path when context-driven hypotheses stall.

claim: Gap status: no source gave a causal test of a code-forced hypothesis-splitting test at equal tokens, no LLM study with implausible rules, no Klahr and Nigam or Alfieri analogue for LLMs, and Klahr, Fay and Dunbar 1993 numbers remain unverified.
agent_test: Run these as our own experiments: forced split-test vs free choice at equal tokens; implausible-rule variant; VOTAT-in-prompt vs free search.
